claims: Theorem (README.md, SPEC.md section 1.1): for every non-square integer N >= 49, with k = floor(sqrt(N)), s(N) >= a(N) = k + sup{delta in (0, 1] : (k + delta)^2 - 4 S*(delta) < N}, where S*(delta) is the largest certified saving alpha_i delta + beta_i over the 34 intervals I_i of intervals.json that contain delta; in closed form a(N) = max{min(2 alpha_i + sqrt(4 alpha_i^2 + N + 4 beta_i - 4 alpha_i k), k + d1_i) : 2 alpha_i + sqrt(...) > k + d0_i}.

The certificate: for each interval a family of line segments defines, for every k >= 7, a C4-symmetric measure on [0, k + delta]^2 of total mass (k + delta)^2 - 4 S(delta) with mass at least 1 on every closed unit square; 136 records (four regions per interval, 187,183,108 leaves) were replayed by replay4d and accepted (4,294 CPU-hours), all 68 families pass structure/validate_family.py, and the published build replayed the eight records of intervals 1 and 34 again.

Corollaries (README.md, SPEC.md section 1.1): a(N) = F(N) = k + 1 at N = (k + 1)^2 - 1 and (k + 1)^2 - 2 and a(N) > F(N) at every other non-square N >= 49, F being Nagamochi's 1 + sqrt(N - 2k + 1) capped at k + 1; a(N) exceeds Karakus's 1/2 + sqrt(N - k + 1/4) except at N = (k + 1)^2 - 1; and, because S*(1) > 3/4, s(n^2 - 1) = s(n^2 - 2) = s(n^2 - 3) = n for n >= 8 without Nagamochi's lemma. The source says these values are not new.

The site write-up (site/src/content/papers/closed-form/en.mdx) adds that for N <= 3600 the bound exceeds the best known lower bound at 3,239 non-square N, equals it at 159 and is below it at 100, by its own table (site/public/data/papers/closed-form-table.csv); it determines s(N) only at (k + 1)^2 - 1, -2 and -3.
